(1) Ocrevus (ocrelizumab, HCPCS J2350), CMS Part B 2025 from the quarterly companion bf6a5b3b-31ee-4abb-b1ad-2607a1e7510a, row '2025 (Q1-Q4)': $633,566,006.34 over 11,393 beneficiaries = $55,610.11 per beneficiary. (2) The ASP ratio of Amgen's own marketed anti-CD20 biosimilar to its reference, from CMS Part B 2024 spending per dosage unit (drug_demand; 2024 is the latest year that carries units): Riabni (Q5123, 10 mg units) $92,447,259.69 over 2,331,225 units = $39.656; Rituxan (J9312, 10 mg units) $436,980,635.10 over 5,729,504.8 units = $76.268. Converted to ASP by the Part B payment rule: Rituxan is paid at ASP + 6%, so its ASP is $71.951; Riabni, a qualifying biosimilar, is paid at its own ASP + 8% of the reference's ASP (Social Security Act 1847A(b)(8) as amended by Inflation Reduction Act s.11403; CMS, 'Frequently Asked Questions: Inflation Reduction Act Biosimilars Temporary Payment Increase', cms.gov/files/document/biosimilar-faqs.pdf), so its ASP is 39.656 - 0.08 x 71.951 = $33.900. Ratio 0.4712. $55,610.11 x 0.4712 = $26,201
column12: Judgement on the discount comparator and year. Riabni is the closest analogue in the book: Amgen's own biosimilar of an infused anti-CD20 antibody paid under Part B. 2024 is its fourth full year. Its payment ratio to Rituxan fell from 0.899 (2021) to 0.655 (2022), 0.561 (2023) and 0.520 (2024) (drug_demand), so a flat price at the year-four level understates the early years and overstates the late ones: Ruxience, the first-wave rituximab biosimilar, was at 0.264 of Rituxan per unit by 2024. Amgen's other Part B biosimilars in 2024, per unit: Mvasi against Avastin 0.36, though Avastin's units include intravitreal eye use, and Kanjinti against Herceptin 0.23. Qian (AJMC 2024, PMID 39745502) finds the rituximab biosimilars' Part B spending per dosage unit fell 15% to 26% in 2022 alone, and Kim et al. (JCO Oncol Pract 2026, PMID 42413074) put bevacizumab biosimilars 52.2% below the originator per administration by 2023. The Ocrevus per-beneficiary figure covers about 0.82 of a patient-year (987 mg per beneficiary in 2024 against a 1,200 mg maintenance year, drug_demand), the house per-beneficiary convention. The 2024 annual figure was $56,845, so 2025 is 2.2% lower

column12: Direction checked: net is $26,201 / 1.06 = $24,718 per patient-year, Ocrevus's 2025 ASP-basis figure ($52,462) x 0.4712. It is the same net the first draft reached by taking Riabni's Part B payment ratio (0.5200) to list and then deducting 14.5% for the 8% add-on on the reference's ASP, restated so the house deduction applies. A 2029 launch would be paid its ASP plus 6% of the reference's ASP, since the 8% rate applies only to biosimilars first paid by 2027-12-31; that changes Medicare's payment, not the ASP the manufacturer realises

column12: The biosimilar's patients are ocrelizumab patients, so ocrelizumab's own persistence applies, not the 28.6% ofatumumab figure the frexalimab seed uses. The case for lower: Engmann et al., JMCP 2021 (PMID 33624535, doi:10.18553/jmcp.2021.20413) find 8% of ocrelizumab starters in PharMetrics Plus stop within 12 months and 17% within 18 months (11.7% a year). The case for higher: both studies are Genentech-funded, and a biosimilar also loses some patients back to the reference: in oncology, 1.2% of patients switched from a biosimilar to the reference (Liu et al., JAMA Oncol 2026, PMID 42658505)

column11: NCT06700343 primary completion 2027-04-19, estimated (ClinicalTrials.gov API v2), plus two gives 2029. But a biosimilar licence cannot take effect until 12 years after the reference's first licensure (PHS Act 351(k)(7)(A)), and Ocrevus (BLA 761053) was first licensed 2017-03-28, so not before 2029-03-28 and 2029 cannot be a full year on sale: 2030 is the first. The book's exclusivities row for Ocrevus (asset 737) carries 2029-03-28 as a '12-year statutory floor' computed from the Purple Book licensure date (backend/fetchers/exclusivity_purplebook.py). BR&R, 'The Early Outlook for Ocrelizumab Biosimilars', 2025-10-21 (biosimilarsrr.com): market exclusivity runs through March 2029 and the primary US patent is expected to expire after October 2028. Amgen gives no launch date
column12: Judgement on timing. A PK/PD readout in 2027 leaves time to file and be approved before the exclusivity date, so launch is expected in 2029 and any revenue from Q2 to Q4 2029 is left out. The case for later: Roche's remaining patents are not checked here, and BPCIA litigation could delay entry; BR&R found no BPCIA proceeding on Ocrevus as of October 2025. Ocrevus Zunovo (subcutaneous, approved 2024-09-13) carries 2036-09-13 in the book, again the computed 12-year floor, and Roche can move patients onto it before 2029; an IV biosimilar cannot substitute for it

column12: Why the revenue route: the engine multiplies its treated stock by the per-beneficiary net price, so revenue over that price is the count the stock must reach to reproduce the reference's IV revenue (104,458 x $52,462 = $5,480mm). The first draft took Ocrevus's share of Medicare disease-modifying-therapy beneficiaries (14,849 of 78,050 in 2024) times the 48.49% of Medicare MS patients on any such therapy (Li J, Hutton GJ, Aparasu RR, Multiple Sclerosis Journal 2025, as the frexalimab seed carries it), 84,312 patients. Its cross-check divided revenue by a full patient-year price rather than the per-beneficiary price the engine uses. The case for lower: Zunovo's share of Ocrevus Part B spending rose from 2.2% in 2025 to 6.8% in Q1 2026 and Roche can convert more before 2029; commercial patients may convert faster than Medicare ones. The case for higher: net revenue per patient sits below ASP for Medicaid and 340B. pool_crowding groups indications only through indication_groups, which holds no multiple sclerosis group, so this asset is not rationed against frexalimab or fenebrutinib. That suits it: its patients are Ocrevus's, not the untreated pool's

column11: Measured class uptake: rituximab biosimilars rose to 60% of all rituximab claims paid by Medicare Part B in 2022, four calendar years after the first US entry (Qian J, Am J Manag Care 2024;30(12):e359-e363, PMID 39745502, doi:10.37765/ajmc.2024.89644). Book path around that anchor: Part B reference claims (Rituxan + Rituxan Hycela, drug_demand) were 197,044 in 2020, 123,181, 91,689, 79,640 and 74,662 in 2024. Holding the total at the 229,222 that Qian's 60% implies for 2022 gives biosimilar shares of 14.0%, 46.3%, 60.0%, 65.3% and 67.4%. Amgen's slice is a third of that: 4.7%, 15.4%, 20.0%, 21.8%, 22.5%. The engine's own identity (incidence 0, 13.4% discontinuation, logistic ramp) was least-squares fitted to those five years. It gives a peak of 0.078, with RMSE 1.9 points, and an engine path of 6.8%, 13.2%, 18.1%, 21.9%, 24.6% of the pool
column12: Judgements, three. (1) One third: three developers run comparative Phase 3 trials against Ocrevus, Amgen (NCT06700343, primary completion 2027-04), Sandoz (CYB704, NCT06847724, 2026-11) and Celltrion (CT-P53, NCT05906992, 2027-02) (ClinicalTrials.gov API v2). Polpharma's PB018 is preclinical (BR&R, 2025-10-21). Amgen reads out last of the three, but all three are held to the same 2029-03-28 exclusivity date, so they can enter together. Entry order decides the slice: in rituximab, Amgen's third-to-market Riabni held about 5% of biosimilar Part B claims in 2022 (6,988 of the 137,534 implied by Qian), against 49% for Ruxience and about 46% for Truxima by residual. That is the case for lower. (2) The class path assumes total rituximab Part B claims held flat from 2020 to 2024, and that Qian's 'all rituximab products' includes Rituxan Hycela. (3) After year 5 the engine keeps capturing, to a 28.9% share of the pool in year 9, above the measured plateau of 22.5%. Meanwhile the zero-incidence pool leaves out new ocrelizumab starts, so the stock falls to 25% by year 15. These two errors pull in opposite directions. Cross-check: Liu et al. (JAMA Oncol 2026, PMID 42658505) find the reference biologics' Medicare Part B market share fell 31.5% a year after biosimilar entry across bevacizumab, rituximab and trastuzumab, a 67.9% biosimilar share by year 3, in line with the path above

column12: The fit puts year-one capture at 88% of peak, so a biosimilar's uptake is close to a step. It behaves like a formulary switch at loss of exclusivity, not a brand launch. The book's MS brand curve (Kesimpta, k 0.735, midpoint 3.62) would badly understate a biosimilar's first three years
